newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: DEADLINE NEARS FOR SOUTH AFRICA APARTHEID AMNESTY.
newsitem.headline: DEADLINE NEARS FOR SOUTH AFRICA APARTHEID AMNESTY.

text.p: Former secret policemen and soldiers were among those making a last-minute rush to apply for amnesty from South Africa's truth commission, officials said on Saturday.
The Truth and Reconciliation Commission, headed by Nobel peace laureate Archbishop Desmond Tutu, wants confessions from all people who might have blood on their hands from the fight over apartheid.
The offer of pardon in exchange for coming clean expires at midnight (2200 GMT) and a spokeswoman said applications were picking up in the hours ahead of the deadline.
"Among the latest were 26 (former) security police...and there are some senior people among them," a commission source told Reuters.
There had also been applications from senior apartheid army officers and the Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party, whose supporters have been reluctant to come forward.
Figures showed a total of around 6,500 people had applied.
The commission refuses to name names, although many politicians have gone on record on their plans.
Inkatha has called the investigation a tool of Nelson Mandela's ruling African National Congress (ANC) intended to wipe out all who oppose it, a charge the commission rejects.
Tutu has made a very public effort to ensure that all parties are heard and treated fairly.
Members of Inkatha fought a decade-long turf war with the ANC in which about 15,000 people were killed. The feud erupted more than a decade ago and is still simmering.

ANC Defence Minister Joe Modise said he would apply but his predecessor, General Magnus Malan, who led the last decade of the white government's fight against black liberation groups said he did not need any pardon.
Malan told the commission on Wednesday he accepted moral responsibility for the army's actions, including raids on ANC targets in neighbouring countries.
"If with the wisdom of hindsight...my authority should be regarded by some as culpable, I am prepared to face the consequences," he said in voluntary testimony.
The commission, which has the power to grant amnesty to those who make full confessions, warned Malan that he might be making a mistake.
"He would be well advised not only in terms of reconciliation but in terms of his own self-interest to apply for amnesty even at this 11th hour," deputy chairman Alex Boraine said on Friday.
The only two surviving former white presidents, P.W. Botha and F.W. de Klerk, also say they committed no crime and have no reason to ask for pardons.
But most of the ANC leadership, with the likely exception of Mandela, were expected to apply and commission sources said over a hundred members made bids in the past day.
The deadline for amnesty applications was originally December last year, but Mandela extended it by five months at Tutu's request because relatively few people had come forward.
Dozens of former security police have since applied, including those responsible for the death of black activist Steve Biko in 1977.
But many others have rejected the probe as a witch hunt, saying that apartheid-era crimes should be forgotten.
They said revelations to the commission hinder rather than help the reconciliation the body is intended to promote.
